# Pacific Communities in Tāmaki Makaurau Auckland

Auckland is home to the largest concentration of Pacific people anywhere in Aotearoa — and indeed, anywhere in the world. With more than 275,000 Pacific people calling the city home, it is a place where Polynesian culture, identity and community life thrive in a uniquely New Zealand context. [[1]](cite://1/1)

![embed-1](embed://1)

## Where Pacific Communities Settled

West and South Auckland have the largest Pacific and Māori communities, while the central city became home to earlier waves of migrants in suburbs like Ponsonby and Grey Lynn. [[2]](cite://2/1) South Auckland, in particular, has more Pacific Islanders living there than any other urban centre in New Zealand. [[3]](cite://3/1) From the 1970s onward, people from across the Pacific settled mainly in the Auckland area, forming communities where they could continue to speak their languages and maintain their customs. [[4]](cite://4/1)

In earlier decades, the inner-city suburbs of Ponsonby and Grey Lynn were at the heart of the Pasifika diaspora, drawing migrants who had come to New Zealand for work in the booming post-war manufacturing sector. [[5]](cite://5/1)

## Who Makes Up the Community

The Pacific population of Auckland — and New Zealand more broadly — is richly diverse. The six largest groups, as of 2018, were Sāmoans, Tongans, Cook Islanders, Fijians, Niueans and Tokelauans. [[6]](cite://6/1) But the community spans far further, with people from Kiribati, Tuvalu, Tahiti, Papua New Guinea, the Solomon Islands, and many other islands also represented. [[4]](cite://4/2)

As Pacific studies lecturer Melani Anae noted in 2001, there is no single 'Pacific community' — rather, Pacific peoples align themselves "variously, and at different times, along ethnic, geographic, church, family, school, age/gender, youth/elders, island born/NZ born, or occupational lines, or a mix of these." [[7]](cite://7/1)

## A Distinct New Zealand Pacific Identity

Over time, something genuinely new has emerged in South Auckland: a distinctive New Zealand Pacific culture that is more than the sum of its parts. [[8]](cite://8/1) Young Pacific people — known variously as PIs, Polys, or New Zealand borns — have developed new music, fashion, customs and ways of speaking, sometimes referred to collectively as *Pasifika Aotearoa*. [[9]](cite://9/1)

![embed-2](embed://2)

Auckland's music scene reflects this creative energy. A strong hip hop culture, first channelled through American Samoa in the 1980s, was revitalised by second and third generation Pacific Islanders in central and South Auckland. Artists such as Che Fu and Nesian Mystik, and the recording label Dawn Raid, have had a lasting influence on mainstream New Zealand music. [[10]](cite://10/1)

Pacific dance has also flourished in Auckland. By the 2000s, the city's Pacific dance community was so large and active it was drawing visitors from around the Pacific. Events like the Pasifika Festival and Polyfest have become major drawcards. [[11]](cite://11/1)

## The Pasifika Festival

One of the most visible expressions of Pacific identity in Auckland is the annual Pasifika Festival at Western Springs. First held in 1993, it has grown into one of the largest celebrations of Pacific culture in the world, showcasing food, music, dance and art from 11 Pacific nations including Sāmoa, Tonga, Fiji, Niue, Tuvalu, the Cook Islands and Aotearoa. [[1]](cite://1/2)[[12]](cite://12/1)

The festival has faced significant challenges over the years — including cancellation following the Christchurch mosque attacks in 2019, pandemic disruptions in 2020, and the aftermath of devastating Auckland floods in 2023 — but has continued to grow and evolve. Festival director Jep Savali has said authenticity is now central to the festival's future, from food offerings to cultural performances. [[13]](cite://13/1)

## A Growing and Young Population

The Pacific population across New Zealand has grown at roughly twice the rate of the overall population. By the 2023 census, Pacific peoples made up 8.9 percent of New Zealand's population — up from 8.1 percent in 2018 — with a median age of just 25, making it a notably young demographic. [[14]](cite://14/1) Former Pacific peoples minister Aupito William Sio has described this growth as confirmation that "Pasifika as well as Māori are the future of New Zealand." [[14]](cite://14/2)

Would you like to explore more about the cultural celebrations and festivals that bring Auckland's Pacific communities together?

7.document_summary: This document explores the rich landscape of cultural dance in New Zealand from the 19th century through the 2000s. European folk dancing was initially dominant but expanded beyond English and Scottish traditions from the 1980s onward. Major cultural events like the Pasifika Festival and Polyfest emerged as among the largest dance festivals in Oceania. Key figures including Prime Minister Peter Fraser, teacher Rae Storey, and dancers Liong Xi and Vivek Kinra promoted these diverse forms. Organizations such as Dance Aotearoa New Zealand (DANZ) and Pacific Dance New Zealand (PDNZ) provided crucial support. By the 21st century, New Zealand's cultural dance scene had become highly diverse with multiple forms taught across schools and cultural centers. Different dance forms increasingly influenced each other and were performed at the same festivals, breaking down traditional boundaries. While cultural dance attracted large audiences and generated economic value, infrastructure remained limited with most events relying on volunteers.

Theatre, dance and kapa haka There are professional theatres in the main centres. 41.document_title: Alistair Te Ariki Campbell: A Distinctive Poetic Voice and Literary Legacy of New Zealand and the Pacific
41.document_summary: Alistair Te Ariki Campbell (1925-2009) was one of New Zealand's most distinctive poets, whose work blended lyricism with darkness shaped by an idyllic Rarotongan childhood, early family tragedies, and exile to New Zealand. Born in Rarotonga, Campbell lost both parents by age eight and spent six years in an orphanage in Dunedin, experiencing racism as a Polynesian in Pākehā New Zealand. He emerged as a significant literary voice in Wellington during the 1950s, publishing his acclaimed first collection "Mine eyes dazzle" (1950). A transformative 1976 return to Rarotonga led Campbell to embrace his Polynesian identity and become a pioneer of Pacific literature, integrating Polynesian and English traditions in works like "The dark lord of Savaiki" (1980). Beyond poetry, Campbell was prolific across genres including autobiography, drama, and children's literature. His Collected Poems (1981) won the New Zealand Book Award for poetry in 1982, while The Frigate Bird was a Commonwealth Writers' Prize regional finalist in 1989. Campbell received numerous honors including the Pacific Islands Artist Award (1998), an honorary doctorate from Victoria University of Wellington (1999), an ONZM (2005), and a Prime Minister's Award for Literary Achievement (2005). He passed away in Wellington Hospital on August 16, 2009, aged 84. Campbell is recognized as a foreparent and active shaper of bicultural and multicultural writing in Aotearoa New Zealand.

42.document_title: Mina Louise McKenzie: Pioneer of Māori-Centered Museum Practice and Her Legacy in New Zealand
42.document_summary: Mina Louise McKenzie (1930-1997) was a pioneering figure in New Zealand's museums sector who revolutionized museum practice by prioritizing mātauranga Māori over western collecting traditions. Born in Palmerston North with tribal affiliations to Ngāti Hauiti, Ngāti Raukawa, Te Ati Haunui-a-Pāpārangi, and Rangitāne o Manawatū, she became the first Māori museum director in New Zealand (1978) while serving as curator and director of Manawatū Museum from the 1970s to 1990s. McKenzie championed bicultural museum practices, emphasizing iwi as kaitiaki (guardians) of taonga tuku iho (treasures), and led major initiatives including the Te Māori exhibition and contributed to Te Papa Tongarewa's development. She served as AGMANZ president (1988-1990) and as an honorary associate lecturer in museum studies at Massey University from 1990. McKenzie held positions on the Manawatū–Wanganui Area Health Board and Historic Places Trust, receiving a Palmerston North Civic Honour Award in 1993. When Manawatū Museum merged with a science centre in 1994, she participated in the transition before retiring in 1995 to assume a kaumatua role. She died suddenly on 11 March 1997, aged 67. Her enduring legacy encompasses advancing Māori professional roles in museums, establishing the Kaitiaki Māori hui, and transforming how New Zealand institutions engage with indigenous collections and communities.

43.document_title: Hilda Phillips: A Critic of Māori Rights and the Anti-Treatyist Tradition in New Zealand
43.document_summary: This biographical and historical analysis examines Hilda Phillips (1922-2006), a prominent conservative critic of Māori land rights and autonomy campaigns in New Zealand. Born in Cape Town to a Jewish family, Phillips emigrated to New Zealand in 1952. When Māori protests intensified in the early 1970s, she became a vocal opponent of remedial legislation and Māori self-determination efforts. Publishing approximately 60 articles between 1974-1981, Phillips argued that special provisions for Māori violated meritocratic principles. Her arguments were heavily criticized by scholars like W.H. Oliver and Keith Sorrenson for unreliable evidence. After 1985, when the Waitangi Tribunal gained retrospective powers, Phillips renewed activism through public speaking and self-published materials like "Let the truth be known" (1988), aligning with the One New Zealand Foundation. In 1989, historian Harry Evison published a comprehensive rebuttal criticizing her arguments about Treaty claims and Māori land ownership as containing misinformation. After her husband Morris died in 1990, Phillips reduced her campaigning due to health issues. She continued publishing through the 1990s and deposited her archive at the Alexander Turnbull Library before her death in 2006. Her work pioneered the "anti-Treatyist" tradition—a body of writing that draws on limited evidence to discredit Māori grievances.

44.document_title: John Logan Campbell: Founding Father of Auckland and His Legacy
44.document_summary: John Logan Campbell (1817-1912) was a Scottish-born entrepreneur who became a founding figure of Auckland, New Zealand. He emigrated to Australia in 1839 and relocated to New Zealand in 1840, where he established Brown and Campbell, Auckland's first merchant firm with partner William Brown. The firm engaged in general merchandise, shipping, and land speculation, allowing Campbell to accumulate substantial wealth as Auckland grew. After a European tour (1848-1850) and marriage to Emma Wilson in 1858, he returned to Auckland in 1871 and became deeply embedded in the financial elite. Campbell founded Auckland's first school of art in 1878 and published his reminiscences, Poenamo (1881), establishing his reputation as a chronicler of Auckland's pioneer era. He served as mayor during the 1901 royal visit and received a knighthood in 1902. His most enduring legacy was gifting 230 acres of his One Tree Hill estate to create Cornwall Park (1902), with additional donations for the park's endowment. Campbell died on 22 June 1912, leaving his residuary estate to charitable and educational causes. His funeral procession to Maungakiekie was notably the largest in Auckland's history.

[Page 1] Agnes TuiSamoa spent a lifetime supporting and campaigning for the rights of her fellow Pacific Islanders in Auckland, both new migrants and their New Zealand born children. She was a leading figure in many community organisations and campaigns, at a time when very few Pacific people were active in the fields of social work or political advocacy. Her work was marked by innovation and a willingness to take a contrary path to others in her community. Her initiatives also supported struggling Auckland families from a variety of other backgrounds. Early life Of Samoan and Chinese descent, Agnes Rosa Sue was born in Suva, Fiji on 7 December 1932, the daughter of Apaula Theresa Perera and her husband, Harry Sue. Her parents separated when she was young and both remarried. Agnes was brought up by her godmother and foster father until the age of 10, when she returned to live with her mother. Her childhood contained many aspects of difference: growing up Samoan in Fiji, with significant links to her Chinese heritage; being Catholic in a largely Protestant country; and being better dressed than many of her schoolmates. These things made her aware that there were many less fortunate than herself. After a Catholic education, she attended a business college and worked for the Catholic bishop as a teenager. In 1951 she moved for a time to Western Samoa, where she consolidated her Samoan language skills. Her facility with languages she also spoke English, Fijian and some Hindi would be very important in later years. She soon became known as someone who could help others, a reputation which followed her to New Zealand. Living in New Zealand Agnes emigrated to New Zealand in 1953 as a young single woman who wanted to become a nurse. She was given a training position at the private Catholic Mater Misericordiae Hospital in Auckland, but faced racism and did not receive the training she had been promised. She resigned and found work in the accounts department at Auckland Hospital’s laundry, which employed many Pacific Islanders. Since the Second World War, the Pacific Island community in Auckland had grown rapidly, its members having travelled to New Zealand looking for increased opportunities for education and employment. In 1954 Agnes had her first child; she was engaged to the boy’s father, but he returned to Western Samoa and she did not wish to follow him. There was minimal social support for unmarried mothers at the time, so others cared for her son on weekdays while she worked. After six months Agnes’ mother took the baby to Fiji. Agnes married Keresipi Tuisamoa in Auckland on 21 October 1955. Born in Western Samoa, Keresipi was a car painter and later a labourer who had emigrated to New Zealand in the early 1950s. Agnes’s second child was born in 1956, and eight more followed over the next 16 years. Her eldest son returned to the family in the early 1960s. The family spelled their surname ‘TuiSamoa’ after Keresipi received a Samoan title in 1998. Social and community work Although Agnes married into the Presbyterian church, her Catholic upbringing remained an important influence throughout her life. She joined the congregation of the Pacific Island Presbyterian Church in Newton, the first Pacific Island church in New Zealand. This church provided social support services to its congregation, and, unlike many other churches at the time, had Pacific Islanders in roles of responsibility. It was also one of the few organisations of the era to work across the quite disparate Pacific migrant communities. Agnes worked voluntarily with the clergy to support those newly arrived from the islands who were struggling to adjust to life in a large city away from their social and kin networks. Unlike many in her community, Agnes felt that attending services on Sunday should be a matter of choice. She viewed her social work and counselling as her contribution to church life. Families increasingly came to Agnes for help her language skills and ability as an advocate created an expectation that she would help people in trouble. She worked as a part time nurse aide in the mid 1960s, but in 1975 she moved into professional community and social work. That year she joined the Auckland Methodist Central Mission; she remained a lynchpin of its Pacific Centre, a unique inner city social service agency run by and for Pacific Islanders, for nearly 30 years. Her work involved assisting families with immigration and legal issues, finance and budgeting, domestic violence, and drug and alcohol problems. She worked with all age groups and ethnicities, often taking on difficult cases, sometimes for years, until they found their feet. She worked with patience and skill, lobbying social welfare officials on behalf of struggling families and working with lawyers on immigration issues. Social work fa’asamoa (in the Samoan way) placed particular demands on Agnes and her family. People would come to her home to seek help, or she would visit theirs, in the middle of the night if necessary. Her young family was also involved, helping provide food to struggling people who came to their door. Agnes received a Certificate for Community Studies from the University of Auckland in 1977. She was later involved in the Pacific Advisory Committee for the new School of Social Work at the Auckland College of Education, working to ensure it met the needs of Pacific Island students. Through her work, Agnes became involved in networks of like minded people in Auckland who were trying to help those in need. She worked particularly closely with urban Pacific Island and Māori groups, and political pressure groups campaigning for the rights of the downtrodden. Agnes was one of the few of the older, more cautious, generation of Pacific Island leaders to support the Polynesian Panther movement, a youth led organisation concerned with the treatment of Pacific Islanders in New Zealand during the 1970s era of ‘dawn raids’ and the deportation of ‘overstayers’. She was regarded as a ‘stirrer’ and likened by some to the Māori women activists of her day, such as Whina Cooper and Eva Rickard . In the early 1970s she also worked with anti racism groups that were exploring the implications of the Treaty of Waitangi. She participated in direct action, particularly supporting tenants at risk of eviction and occupying homes while legal issues were resolved. She was also involved in a successful legal challenge to New Zealand’s immigration policies in 1982, which reclassified many Western Samoans as New Zealand citizens. Social organisations As well as assisting families directly, Agnes helped pioneer and support many social organisations, as the needs of Auckland’s Pacific Island community changed over the decades. Much of this work was focused on Auckland’s inner suburbs such as Grey Lynn, Ponsonby and Herne Bay, where the Tuisamoa family and most of the city’s Pacific Islanders lived at the time. In 1978 she helped establish the Grey Lynn Neighbourhood Law Office, which provided free legal advice. This was the first community law centre in the country; such centres soon became an important part of New Zealand’s legal culture. Recognising that there was a lack of culturally appropriate services for vulnerable members of Pacific Island and Māori communities, Agnes helped set up or support three women’s refuges, an organisation to assist alcoholics, the Grey Lynn Community Housing Society, a residential housing programme for homeless young people, and Pillars, an organisation supporting children whose parents were in prison. Agnes believed that the education system was letting down Pacific Island children by undermining their culture. She considered language central to defining a person’s identity, so was concerned for the New Zealand born generations of Pacific Islanders living without their language: ‘They will think of themselves as Kiwi, but will Kiwis accept them? I don’t think so. They will be in limbo.’ 1 In the 1980s she helped establish the first full immersion Pacific Island language early childhood centre in Auckland, A’oga Fa’a Samoa, a model since replicated around the country. Disappointed that her own children had not grown up bilingual, she took much pleasure in interacting with her Samoan speaking grandchildren. She was also involved with the governance of her children’s schools, and took part in initiatives to promote non formal and community education initiatives for adults. Agnes sat on many committees which advised local and central government. She was a member of the Samoan Council of Women and the Pacific Islands Advisory Council, established to create lines of communication between her community, the Minister of Pacific Island Affairs and government. She also worked in the Labour Party’s Auckland Central electorate office. She represented New Zealand at the 1975 Pacific Women’s Conference in Suva, the first time women in the region came together to assess the position of women in their societies. From this grew a new women’s organisation, PACIFICA, which aimed to empower Pacific women living in New Zealand. In 1988 she was one of the first trustees appointed to the ASB Community Trust, an organisation which provided grants to groups in Auckland and Northland. She held this position until 1994. Later life and legacy Agnes stood out for taking on non traditional roles, particularly as a woman in Auckland’s largely conservative Samoan community. She was the first Pacific Island woman in many community organisations. She believed strongly in the equality of men and women, and stood up to those who sought to play down social issues within their community. Likewise, she took a contrary view to many in her generation with regard to the cultural obligations on families to donate money to the church and extended family members in the islands. Her belief that her children should have freedom sometimes brought her into conflict with her more traditional husband. Made a Justice of the Peace in 1985, Agnes enjoyed the opportunity this role gave her to meet a range of people. She did not wish to receive public recognition for her work, but was awarded a Queen’s Service Medal for community service in 1985. She retired from social work in the early 2000s, at a time when professional social work was changing radically. Although she was dedicated to Samoan culture, Agnes lived in New Zealand for 51 years. Interviewed in 1988, she said that she defined herself as a New Zealander and regarded New Zealand as her home. She also denied that she was a ‘leader’ of her community, or even a ‘helper’: ‘I don’t claim to lead people, I want to walk along with them, I don’t want to get in front’. 2 She died in Auckland on 17 November 2004, aged 71, and was survived by her husband and children.

[Page 1] Te Pahi was by 1800 one of the senior chiefs of the north western Bay of Islands. He was the son of Wharerau, a descendant of the ancient ancestral Ngāti Awa, the original people of the area, and of their Ngāpuhi conquerors, a combination which gave him great mana over the land and its people. He was related to Ngāti Rēhia, and probably to Te Hikutū and Ngāti Rua. Te Pahi's principal pā was on a small island called Te Puna or Te Pahi's island, situated between Rangihoua Bay and Moturoa. He usually resided at the inlet nearby, but he kept his weapons store and other treasures on Te Puna. In 1805 his closest relatives were living on the island under his brother 'Tiarrah'. Te Pahi had several wives, one of whom he put to death for her venomous tongue, and at least four sons and three or more daughters. He kept one of his daughters confined for several years in a small storehouse on Te Puna; she was a high born woman reserved for an important marriage alliance. Another daughter, Atahoe, married George Bruce, a European castaway. After a voyage to India he abandoned her (she was then known as Mary Bruce) in Port Jackson (Sydney), New South Wales, where she died in 1810, leaving a daughter in the Female Orphan School. One of Te Pahi's sons, Matara, travelled to England in 1807, where he met George III, and returned to New Zealand in 1809. In 1805 Te Pahi and four of his sons took passage in a small colonial vessel, the Venus, intending to visit Philip King, lieutenant governor of Norfolk Island; King's reputation for generosity towards the Māori attracted Te Pahi. However, the master of the vessel ill treated his passengers and threatened to retain Te Pahi's eight year old son to pay for their passages. At Norfolk Island the commandant, Captain John Piper, rescued the boy and welcomed the visitors. Hearing that Te Pahi wished to visit King, now governor of New South Wales, Piper helped him to obtain passages to Port Jackson in the Buffalo; the group arrived there on 27 November 1805. Te Pahi, the first influential Māori leader to visit New South Wales, and the proprietor of a safe anchorage frequented by the colony's whaling ships, was of value to King. With the safety and comfort of European visitors to New Zealand in mind, King spared no effort to convince Te Pahi of the benefits of an association with Europeans. Te Pahi and his sons were guests at Government House during their three month stay. The chief was presented with iron tools, fruit tree seedlings, livestock and many other gifts. He was also given a small prefabricated house to erect in a safe place under his protection, for the use of European visitors to the Bay of Islands. For his part Te Pahi gave the governor a number of fine cloaks and a stone mere. Te Pahi was keenly interested in a cultural and technological exchange. He suggested that several of his people should visit New South Wales to learn the skills of shepherds (a meeting with the influential sheepbreeder John McArthur probably prompted this interest). He welcomed King's plan to settle an official party of observers for a few months under his protection at Te Puna, a plan which came to nothing when King was replaced by William Bligh. Many European customs and institutions shocked and disgusted Te Pahi; he was horrified by the severity of sentencing in cases of minor theft. He also had scant tolerance for those Aborigines he encountered, and was critical of their mode of (un)dress, their weapons and way of life.

47.document_title: Norman Eric Kirk: New Zealand's Labour Prime Minister - Political Biography and Legacy
47.document_summary: This biographical account traces Norman Eric Kirk's remarkable political journey from his working-class origins to becoming New Zealand's fourth Labour Prime Minister. Born in 1923 in Waimate, South Canterbury, Kirk rose from humble beginnings as a roof painter, railway worker, and boiler engineer to become a transformative political figure. After joining the Labour Party in 1943, he served as mayor of Kaiapoi from 1953, implementing progressive infrastructure reforms. Elected to Parliament in 1957 representing Lyttelton, Kirk distinguished himself as an excellent debater and advocate for constituents and the disadvantaged. He ascended through Labour ranks, becoming party vice president in 1963 and president in 1964, before defeating Arnold Nordmeyer on December 9, 1965, to become leader of the parliamentary Labour Party at age 42. His 1969 campaign slogan "Make things happen" emphasized planned economic development, though he narrowly lost to Keith Holyoake. Labour's 1972 electoral victory brought Kirk to the Prime Minister's office, where his government pursued activist policies including establishing diplomatic relations with China, opposing racial discrimination, and resisting nuclear testing. However, global economic slowdown, oil price increases, and rising inflation undermined his ambitious agenda. Kirk's health deteriorated following a grueling international tour and leg surgery in April 1974. Despite declining health, he continued working through mounting industrial unrest until his death from congestive cardiac failure on August 31, 1974, at age 51. Kirk left a lasting legacy as Labour's last passionate advocate for big government.

48.document_summary: Charles Philippe Hippolyte de Thierry (b. 1793) was a French-born adventurer and would-be colonizer who pursued ambitious schemes to establish settlements in New Zealand. Born to an exiled French family during the Revolution, he claimed to have purchased 40,000 acres at Hokianga through missionary Thomas Kendall in 1822. After failed attempts to secure government backing from Britain, the Dutch, and France, Thierry traveled to America and eventually reached New Zealand in 1837 aboard the Nimrod. Though Māori chiefs repudiated the original land purchase and granted him only 800 acres, he established a small settlement. His grandiose claims of being a sovereign chief were undermined by reports from explorers like Robert FitzRoy. After the Treaty of Waitangi (1840) ended colonial prospects, Thierry relocated to Auckland, where he lived modestly, teaching music and pursuing various business ventures including flax processing. He died in Auckland in 1864, having written an autobiography presenting himself as New Zealand's principal pioneer colonist.

49.document_summary: William Fitzgerald Crawford (1844-1915) was an Irish-born entrepreneur and pioneering photographer who emigrated to New Zealand in 1864. After working various jobs including bushman and goldminer, he established himself in Gisborne as a brewer, becoming the town's first mayor in 1877. Despite bankruptcy in 1882, he rebuilt his brewery business and became renowned for his extensive photographic documentation of Gisborne and Poverty Bay using wet-plate and dry-plate processes. Crawford's photography captured the district's people, places, and events from the 1880s onward, with hundreds of large plates and thousands of quarter-plates surviving. Known for his genial nature and scientific interests, Crawford also pursued various inventions. He left Gisborne in 1913 and died in Auckland in 1915, leaving behind a significant photographic legacy of 19th-century New Zealand.

50.document_summary: James Dilworth (1815-1894) was an Irish-born entrepreneur who emigrated to New Zealand in 1839. After working as a bank accountant in Auckland, he became a successful land speculator and farmer, accumulating substantial property holdings worth £81,044 by 1882. Though a major land speculation venture in the Thames Valley resulted in significant losses (estimated £40,000+), Dilworth remained solvent while six other speculators became insolvent. He was a reserved but loyal man who married Isabella Hall in 1853. Dilworth had an impressive record of public service, serving as a trustee of the Auckland Savings Bank for 27 years, on the Auckland Provincial Council, and supporting education and social causes. Upon his death in 1894, his estate valued at £150,000 was bequeathed to establish the Dilworth Ulster Institute Trust, which created Dilworth School—ultimately becoming one of New Zealand's largest boarding schools.

Aansan Yen, who has Chinese heritage but was born and raised in the Netherlands, said she was intrigued by and interested in Pasific Island cultures. "I love to see the dance, the artistry, and I also feel a strong connection to the ocean," she said. https://www.r nz.co.nz/national/programmes/saturday/audio/2018978001/live from th e pasifika festival "It's important to celebrate unity, tradition, community all the things that make life important for me." Political leaders also made an appearance, and the leader of the opposition Chris Hipkins said the festival was a chance to connect with different Pasifika communities in one place. "Pasifika communities make up such a big part of Aotearoa's overall culture and identity. We are of the Pacific," he said. "I think political leaders have got a really important job in bringing the community together. That means celebrating our differences." Pasifika Festival runs from 9am to 6pm on Saturday 8 March and 10am to 4pm on Sunday 9 March. The festival was cancelled in 2019 following the Christchurch mosque attacks, then again in 2020 due to the Covid 19 pandemic. In 2023 the festival went ahead but took a very different tone, held just weeks after storms devastated much of Auckland. Major Events from Tātaki Auckland Unlimited's festival director and group manager Jep Savali said Pasifika Festival is now on a "growth curve". Authenticity had become an important topic in discussions with the Pasifika Village Charitable Trust, which advised on the cultural integrity of the festival. "In our feedback to each other about how we can be better, where we can once again grow this festival, authenticity is really important. Authenticity of food offering, authenticity in terms of the cultural exchange, in terms of the performances." Alf Filipaina, Manukau ward councillor, fondly recalls the festival's early days and attending with his Samoan perspective. "I remember when they started the Pasifika Festival at Western Springs, way back in the day, the first one," he said. "You look and see your Samoan side of who you are performing, with the songs they sing and the performances." Filipaina also emphasised the importance of experiencing other Pacific cultures. He points to Polyfest, another key event, as an example of celebrating cultural richness through its eight diverse villages. "Watching our leaders of the future perform at Polyfest it's amazing. And it's not just about your own culture, but about learning something from other people's cultures too. That's why I love it." The festival's food is a major drawcard for the community, he says. "People should definitely try the food. Honestly, I eat too much of it, especially the panikeke. Oh, the banana one it's shocking, but we love our food." The two day celebration is family friendly event. Festival goers can expect to experience the richness of Pacific culture, language, and identity through over 1,000 performers from 11 Pacific countries including Aotearoa, Cook Islands, Fiji, Hawai'i, Niue, Samoa, Tokelau, and Tonga. The event will feature live music, dance, arts and crafts, traditional food, and hands on cultural experiences. Performances include youth showcases like Gafoa Le Ata from Kōwhai Intermediate, routines by The Royal Family Dance Crew, and soulful music by Samoan artist Vaniah Toloa. Pacific drumming and choir performances will also fill the festival with powerful rhythms. There will also be a Q&A with Miki Magasiva, director of film Tinā, and a performance by the rising R&B Fijian group LeftOvas LiveBand, who recently featured as the opening act for SIX60 after winning the Moana Music Open Mic Competition. A range of interactive workshops and cultural experiences include Mophead Storytelling with Dr. Selina Tusitala Marsh, traditional wood carving with Jim Stretton, and a live mural art collaboration with John Crouch and Jim To'o Stretton. While Filipaina has made it known that his favourite is the banana panikeke, those attending Pasifika can indulge in a variety of authentic Pacific dishes including Tongan 'ota ika, Fijian kokoda, and Niuean takihi. The festival will also feature island style barbecues, traditional hangi and umu feasts. Pasifika Vibes at MOTAT will offer ukulele lessons, children's activities, and live cultural performances. Plan ahead for travel Public transport is recommended, with trains and buses running. Although some bus routes will be diverted due to road closures. "We also found that when Pacific people marry outside of [their culture], they will marry a Māori first," Gerardine Clifford Lidstone, the Secretary for Pacific Peoples at MPP, told Khalia Strong on Pacific Mornings. [Page 1] Indo Fijians 'struggling for identity' in Aotearoa voice concerns about ethnicity classification ByLydia Lewis RNZ Pacific Journalist 2024 11 01 11:58:19+13:00 Fiji's Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka says that as far as Fiji is concerned, Fijians of Indian descent are Fijian. While Fiji is part of the Pacific, Indo Fijians are not classified as Pacific peoples in New Zealand; instead, they are listed under Indian and Asian on the Stats NZ website. "The 'Fijian Indian' ethnic group is currently classified under 'Asian,' in the subcategory 'Indian', along with other diasporic Indian ethnic groups," Stats NZ told RNZ Pacific. "This has been the case since 2005 and is in line with an ethnographic profile that includes people with a common language, customs, and traditions. "Stats NZ is aware of concerns some have about this classification, and it is an ongoing point of discussion with stakeholders." The Fijian Indian community in Aotearoa has long opposed this and raised the issue again at a community event Rabuka attended in Auckland's Māngere ahead of the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) in Samoa last month. "As far as Fiji is concerned, [Indo Fijians] are Fijians," he said. When asked what his message to New Zealand on the issue would be, he said: "I cannot; that is a matter of sovereignty, the sovereign decision by the government of New Zealand. What they call people is their sovereign right. As far as we are concerned, we hope that they will be treated as Fijians." More than 60,000 people were transferred from all parts of British India to work in Fiji between 1879 and 1916 as indentured labourers. Today, they make up over 32 percent of the total population, according to Fiji Bureau of Statistics' 2017 Population Census. Now many, like Sangam community NZ leader and former Nadi Mayor Salesh Mudaliar, say they are more Fijian than Indian. "If you do a DNA or do a blood test, we are more of Fijian than anything else. We are not Indian," Mudaliar said. The indenture labourers, who came to be known as the Girmitiyas, as they were bound by a girmit a Hindi pronunciation of the English word "agreement". RNZ Pacific had approached the Viti Council e Aotearoa for their views on the issue. However, they refused to comment, saying that its chair "has opted out of this interview." "Topic itself is misleading bordering on disinformation [and] misinformation from an Indigenous Fijian perspective and overly sensitive plus short notice." 'Struggling for identity' "We are Pacific Islanders. If you come from Tonga or Samoa, you are a Pacific Islander," Mudaliar said. "When [Indo Fijians] come from Fiji, we are not. We are not a migrant to Fiji. We have been there for [over 140] years." "The community is still struggling for its identity here in New Zealand…we are still not [looked after]. He said they have tried to lobby the New Zealand government for their status but without success. "Now it is the National government, and no one seems to be listening to us in understanding the situation. "If we can have an open discussion on this, coming to the same table, and knowing what our problem is, then it would be really appreciated." Lifting quality of data Stats NZ said it is aware of the need to lift the quality of ethnicity data across the government data system. "Public consultation in 2019 determined a need for an in depth review of the Ethnicity Standard," the data agency said. In 2021, Stats NZ undertook a large scoping exercise with government agencies, researchers, iwi Māori, and community groups to help establish the scope of the review. Stats NZ subsequently stood up an expert working group to progress the review. "This review is still underway, and Stats NZ will be conducting further consultation, so we will have more to say in due course," it said. "Classifying ethnicity and ethnic identity is extremely complex, and it is important Stats NZ takes the time to consult extensively and ensure we get this right," the agency added. This week, Fijians celebrate the Hindu festival of lights, Diwali. The nation observes a public holiday to mark the day, and Fijians of all backgrounds get involved. Prime Minister Rabuka's message is for all Fijians to be kind to each other. "Act in accordance with the spirit of Diwali and show kindness to those who are going through difficulties," he told local reporters outside parliament on Thursday. Born to a Māori mother and Samoan father from Moata'a village, Kaka grew up largely disconnected from both cultures. Motivated by the arrival of her baby boy and encouragement from her grandmother, she has committed to attending weekly Samoan lessons to ensure she can pass on cultural knowledge and language to the next generation. The article highlights Kaka's emphasis on the importance of learning language, understanding aganuu (cultural customs), and maintaining meaningful connection to her people and roots. Additionally, Kaka expresses her interest in representing Samoa's rugby team in the future and offers practical advice to others embarking on their own language learning journeys, encouraging consistency and full embrace of their cultural identity.

[Page 1] The Cook Islands secretary of culture Emile Kairua says people in his country are getting complacent about the use of Māori. Cook Islands Māori Language Week started on Sunday in New Zealand and will run until Saturday. Kairua said the language is at risk at the source. "Here in the homeland, we're complacent," he told RNZ Pacific. "People have stopped using it in their everyday lives. Even my children, I must admit, don't speak Cook Islands Māori. They understand it, thankfully, but they can't speak it." Kairua said he thinks Cook Islands Māori is stronger in Aotearoa because that is where a lot of the language teachers are living. "We haven't done a welfare audit of the language in Aotearoa [but] I would imagine that it's a lot stronger, purely because a lot of our teachers, a lot of our orators, are living in Aotearoa. https://www.rnz.co. nz/international/programmes/datelinepacific/audio/2018998039/cook isl anders reflect on nation s 60th milestone "I guess being away from the source, being away from home, there is a feeling of homesickness, so that you do tend to grab onto to what you're missing." He said it was "critical" that Cook Islanders "wake up and appreciate the importance of our language and make sure that it's not a dying part of our identity". "A race without a language they don't have an identity. So as Cook Islanders, either first, second or third generation, we need to hold on to this." Ministry of Pacific Peoples secretary Gerardine Clifford Lidstone said there is power in our language it anchors identity and builds belonging. The theme of the week, ''Ātui'ia au ki te vaka o tōku matakeinanga', translates to 'connect me to the offerings of my people'. The Cook Islands Māori community is the third largest Pacific group in Aotearoa New Zealand. [Page 1] A growing youthful population of Māori and Pasifika is the future of Aotearoa New Zealand, a former Pacific peoples minister says. https://w ww.rnz.co.nz/international/programmes/datelinepacific/audio/20189405 14/nz census shows an increase in pacific population Stats NZ data from the latest census has revealed an increase in Pacific population groups from 8.1 in 2018 to 8.9 percent in 2023. It also showed the median age for Pacific people is 25. The former minister and community leader Aupito William Sio said the data is a confirmation. "I have always known for a very long time that we are a very fast growing population which paints a picture that Pasifika as well as Māori are the future of New Zealand," he said. The Pasifika population has grown rapidly, about twice the rate of New Zealand's population, according to 2006 2023 census data. Pacific people now make up 442,632 people compared to 381,642 in 2018. The New Zealand population has grown to nearly five million in total. The matter of Indo Fijians/Fijian Indians claiming Pacific Islander in the census as their ethnicity must also be considered, Fiji Girmit NZ president Krish Naidu said, noting what has been a long standing issue. "They do have a Fijian passport. I will always include them but there is a different matter when it comes to Fijian. They are divided and it is a matter," Sio said. RNZ Pacific asked the Minister for Pacific Peoples Dr Shane Reti on whether Indo Fijians were included in Ministry of Pacific Peoples as Pacific people. In a statement, his office said: "The Ministry for Pacific Peoples is undertaking ongoing policy work to better understand this issue." During this month's Girmit celebrations in Auckland, Prime Minister Chris Luxon did not address the issue despite "clarity" being directly called from this coalition government being called for by the Girmit community. Under the coalition government there is no Pacific representation in Parliament. Budget and tax cuts Meanwhile, around 5000 public sector roles have been axed by the coalition government's priority to make national tax cuts. Over 60 jobs from the Ministry for Pacific Peoples are included in this, but 31 roles were already vacant. "The job cuts at the moment is causing uncertainty, it is causing a real sense of low morale within the public sector workforce," Sio said. "It's tough times for many facing redundancies." RNZ Pacific has spoken to one public sector worker who did not wish to be named. They had already lost "two jobs in one year." After the elections, they wanted to "create change" and help their community by working within the public sector. Despite many of their colleagues leaving because they did not align with the values of New Zealand new coalition leaders, they said staying in good faith has resulted in her job being on the line. The public sector worker said it was a "disappointing" outcome. Sio said he felt "suspicious about New Zealand's upcoming budget" and was unaware of Pacific community leaders being invited to any pre or post budget events. Following last year's scrutiny over a pre budget breakfast blowout, the Ministry of Pacific Peoples was criticised by ACT leader David Seymour for "overspending" taxpayer money. Opposition's deputy leader of Labour and spokesperson for Pacific peoples Carmel Sepuloni has been approached for comment. [Page 1] 'You're not a nobody': Auckland student embraces Solomon Islands heritage ByTiana Haxton Journalist, Coco Lance RNZ Pacific Digital Journalist 2025 11 28 13:40:23+13:00 Feature A student from St Pauls primary school in Auckland says his Solomon Islands heritage is his identity. Solomon Islands Pidgin Language Week is being celebrated across New Zealand, under the theme "Protektim langguis an kalsa blong yumi Protect our language and culture." To mark the occasion, the Solomon Islands Auckland Wantok Association Inc visited Bruce Satchell's primary school to share a cultural showcase with his classmates. Eleven year old Satchell is proud to hail from seven different cultures, including the Solomon Islands. He said learning about his indigenous heritage is how he connects to his identity. "It's really important because I get to know my family history and my indigenous part of my life. It's just very important to know where you're from, and like, you're not a nobody. So like a somebody, yeah." Satchell's cousins were amongst the performers sharing traditional Solomon Islands dances for the students of St Pauls primary. For the sixth grader, sharing his culture makes him feel proud of who he is. "Well, today was like, magical, seeing everyone like perform and give their best. Yeah, it was really good... I feel powerful and proud and glad to be here." The chair of the Auckland Wantok Association said it is vital to encourage young ones to connect with their heritage. Florie Dausabea was proud to support Bruce in sharing his Solomon Islands culture with his peers. "It reinforces and reaffirms who he is, his identity and his culture and custom. And I think that is very important. It is the essence of why we celebrate Solomon Islands language week." St Pauls primary caters to students between five and eleven years old. With a roll of 470, the school hosts a diverse spread of cultures. Principal Mary Zellman said it is vital the school takes every opportunity to celebrate everyone's heritage. "I really feel very strongly that we need to celebrate different people's cultures and have pride in our own cultures by celebrating everybody's cultures." "It's really important that we know who we are and where we come from, and that needs to be, that has to be acknowledged, because we're all human beings, We're all Special. We're all unique." Deputy principal Angelina Brayne echoed her sentiments, saying they want to foster cultural pride amongst all their students. This was something she saw in action as former students were amongst the performers on stage. "It was a privilege, an absolute honor, and to see our past pupils, also to be part of the cultural group and to go on from St Paul's School and to be proud of who they are, strong and their identity. That's what we want for all our tamariki." The Deo sisters have fond memories of their time at St Pauls primary. They said the teachers always encouraged them to be proud of their heritage. Ebony Deo was excited to return to embrace and show off their culture. "I'm very happy to show my culture to… my past teachers as well, to see like, how well I've done and how proud I am." Her elder sister Jolenna said being able to encourage the young students to embrace their indigenous languages is vital. "I think it's fundamental. I think it's incredibly important. I think language tells you a lot about who you are and the people that you come from, and gives you a sense of belonging... so language, to me, is like at the core of a lot of our culture." Solomon Islands is a predominantly Melanesian nation that has more than 70 indigenous languages and dialects on Melanesian and Polynesian origin. In this culturally diverse context, Pidgin has a unifying effect in that it is spoken by Solomon Islanders throughout the country. This year is only the second edition of the Solomon Islands Pidgin Language week runs through until Satruday. It is the last event on the Ministry of Pacific Peoples New Zealand language week series calendar. Related

This comprehensive guide explores Auckland, New Zealand's largest metropolitan region with 1.42 million residents (one-third of the national population). The document covers Auckland's diverse geography featuring two harbours, 49 volcanic cones, and 1,613 kilometres of coastline. As a multicultural metropolis where Asians, Pacific Islanders, and Māori comprise 48% of residents, Auckland is the world's largest Polynesian city.

The guide traces Auckland's history from early Māori settlement through European colonization beginning in the 1820s, establishment as New Zealand's capital in 1840, the kauri timber industry boom (1870-1900), and transformation into a modern industrial and commercial center. It documents significant immigration waves including Irish settlers, post-WWII British immigrants, Māori rural-to-urban migration, Vietnamese refugees, and Asian migrants.

Geologically, Auckland features ancient greywacke basement rock and volcanic eruptions dating from 150,000 years ago to Rangitoto's eruption 600 years ago. The region's warm, moderately wet climate supports native vegetation including kauri forests and pōhutukawa trees, alongside over 600 introduced exotic species.

The document covers contemporary development as a primate city, urban sprawl, motorway development, and economic shifts from manufacturing to services. It details vibrant cultural institutions, sports venues like Eden Park, and the "City of Sails" sailing culture. The guide addresses government structure (unified council since 2010), education (558 schools plus tertiary institutions), healthcare development, and contemporary challenges including traffic congestion and housing affordability.

5.fileDescription: This comprehensive document examines the systemic deportation and racial discrimination faced by Pasifika New Zealanders through the "dawn raids" of the 1970s-1980s. Initially encouraged to migrate for manufacturing jobs, Pacific Islanders faced targeted persecution when the economy declined. Despite comprising only one-third of overstayers, Pasifika people made up two-thirds of prosecutions. Police conducted racially-targeted raids on homes, workplaces, bars, and churches, detaining people based on appearance rather than legal status, affecting even New Zealand citizens and legal residents from Cook Islands, Tokelau, and Niue. The Polynesian Panthers emerged in 1971 as a resistance movement inspired by the American Black Panther Party. Founded by six young activists including Melani Anae, the Panthers fought racism through peaceful resistance, community programs, legal education, and counter-raids on politicians' homes. The piece highlights the Panthers' 50-year legacy and their continued advocacy efforts, including a 10,000-signature petition to the Immigration Minister and educational programs in schools. It documents current vulnerabilities faced by undocumented migrants and the government's formal apology announced for June 26, 2021. The Panthers continue their mission through community education, emphasizing that education remains the strongest form of protest against systemic injustice.

chunkHighlights.text: While Pasifika communities comprised a minority of migrants to New Zealand—eclipsed by migrants from Europe, North America and Australia—they were highly visible and easily scapegoated, much like the Chinese immigrants before them. “The myth was that Pasifika
people were stealing jobs,” says activist Alec Toleafoa. “That we were responsible for the violent crime, and that we were largely to blame for the country’s economic woes.”

For the Pasifika community, the crackdown on immigration status came as a surprise. Previously, the authorities hadn’t seemed to care about overstayers. “They were quite happy to waive the immigration documentation while things were going good,” says Toleafoa, “but once the economy busted, then they started to enforce immigration laws.”
Central Auckland suburbs such as Ponsonby and Grey Lynn were at the heart of the Pasifika diaspora. A marching group entertains crowds on Samoan Day at Grey Lynn Park on January 26, 1974.

7.fileDescription: This comprehensive document examines New Zealand's rapidly transforming society through ethnic diversity, urban development, and demographic shifts. Since the 1987 Immigration Act, New Zealand has become one of the most ethnically diverse nations with 213 ethnic groups. Auckland, hosting 40% of ethnic migrants, is now more diverse than Sydney, London, or Los Angeles, with Asian populations at 23% expected to overtake Maori as the largest ethnic minority by the 2020s. The document explores how diversity has manifested geographically through 'ethnoburbs' and ethnic precincts, exemplified by Northcote's transformation into an 80% Asian business district. New Zealand faces significant demographic challenges: single-person households have risen from one in ten to one in four, family structures have fundamentally shifted, and urban growth is heavily concentrated in major cities while many regional areas face permanent decline. Examples include Waiouru declining from 1,647 to 738 residents between 2001-2013, and Ruapehu District declining 12% since 2006. Rising income inequality grew faster than most OECD countries between 1985-2008, with the top 10% earning nine times more than the bottom 10%. Urban spatial segregation is increasing, with wealthy residents moving to city centers while lower-income populations are pushed to peripheries, creating housing affordability crises. The analysis contrasts compact urban intensification versus greenfield sprawl approaches. New Zealand's attitudes toward Asian immigration have warmed significantly since the 1990s, though challenges including stereotyping and workplace discrimination persist. Resilience across New Zealand's diverse communities will be essential for navigating the future.

Key developments include: the emergence of distinct identity through cultural markers like the All Blacks rugby team's 1905 victory and Edmund Hillary's Everest climb; the impact of World Wars I and II on national consciousness; the development of Pākehā culture characterized by beach culture, bush appreciation, and rugby traditions; and transformation from bicultural to multicultural society through immigration from Pacific Islands, Asia, Africa, and the Middle East. 9.fileDescription: This comprehensive document examines Tongan migration to New Zealand and community development from the 1960s onwards. By 2018, over 82,000 Tongans lived in New Zealand, with two-thirds born there, making them the second-largest Pacific ethnic group, primarily settled in Auckland's Ōtara and Māngere. Despite socio-economic challenges including lower median incomes ($21,000 vs $40,000 nationally), overcrowded housing, and lower employment rates, Tongans maintain strong cultural identity through churches, language, and family traditions rooted in anga faka-Tonga. The document explores how Tongan culture blends traditional values of respect, obedience, and reciprocal sharing with Christian beliefs introduced by Methodist missionaries in the 1820s. It identifies three distinct Tongan groups: those maintaining traditional anga faka-Tonga, New Zealand-born Tongans with decreasing language knowledge, and those identifying with broader Pacific Islander identity. Language preservation challenges are evident, with Tongan-speaking population declining from 63% (1996) to 40% (2018). The document highlights the emergence of Pasifika Aotearoa—a new cultural identity blending Pacific traditions with Afro-American influences, hip-hop, and reggae. 10.fileDescription:
This comprehensive guide explores Auckland, New Zealand's largest metropolitan region with 1.42 million residents (one-third of the national population). The document covers Auckland's diverse geography featuring two harbours, 49 volcanic cones, and 1,613 kilometres of coastline. As a multicultural metropolis where Asians, Pacific Islanders, and Māori comprise 48% of residents, Auckland is the world's largest Polynesian city.

The guide traces Auckland's history from early Māori settlement through European colonization beginning in the 1820s, establishment as New Zealand's capital in 1840, the kauri timber industry boom (1870-1900), and transformation into a modern industrial and commercial center. It documents significant immigration waves including Irish settlers, post-WWII British immigrants, Māori rural-to-urban migration, Vietnamese refugees, and Asian migrants.

Geologically, Auckland features ancient greywacke basement rock and volcanic eruptions dating from 150,000 years ago to Rangitoto's eruption 600 years ago. The region's warm, moderately wet climate supports native vegetation including kauri forests and pōhutukawa trees, alongside over 600 introduced exotic species.

The document covers contemporary development as a primate city, urban sprawl, motorway development, and economic shifts from manufacturing to services. It details vibrant cultural institutions, sports venues like Eden Park, and the "City of Sails" sailing culture. The guide addresses government structure (unified council since 2010), education (558 schools plus tertiary institutions), healthcare development, and contemporary challenges including traffic congestion and housing affordability.

Hip-hop artists such as Che Fu and Nesian Mystik and the recording label Dawn Raid have influenced mainstream popular music.

11.fileDescription: This document explores the rich landscape of cultural dance in New Zealand from the 19th century through the 2000s. It traces how immigrant communities brought diverse dance traditions including Pacific Island dances (tamure, lakalaka, siva), European styles (Scottish reels, Irish dancing, English folk dancing, Polish, Greek), and Asian forms (Balinese legong, Indian bharata natyam and kathak, Chinese lion and dragon dances). European folk dancing was initially dominant but expanded beyond English and Scottish traditions from the 1980s onward. Major cultural events like the Pasifika Festival and Polyfest emerged as among the largest dance festivals in Oceania. Key figures including Prime Minister Peter Fraser, teacher Rae Storey, and dancers Liong Xi and Vivek Kinra promoted these diverse forms. Organizations such as Dance Aotearoa New Zealand (DANZ) and Pacific Dance New Zealand (PDNZ) provided crucial support. By the 21st century, New Zealand's cultural dance scene had become highly diverse with multiple forms taught across schools and cultural centers. Different dance forms increasingly influenced each other and were performed at the same festivals, breaking down traditional boundaries. While cultural dance attracted large audiences and generated economic value, infrastructure remained limited with most events relying on volunteers.

By the 2000s the Pacific dance community (especially in Auckland) was so large and active that it attracted visitors from around the Pacific. Auckland’s Pasifika Festival and Polyfest drew huge audiences. Pacific Dance New Zealand ran dance classes and the Pacific Dance Fono.

"They don't have the money nor the labour force to be able to provide so the kids who were part of Aoga Amata previously, and have grown up with Fa'asamoa, the current crop don't have that simply because there is no Aoga Amata." Vaai believed that the strong foundations that once supported Gagana Samoa in New Zealand, were no longer there.
